items.stem: What are the three areas of exploration in the course?
items.answer: Readers, writers and texts; Time and space; Intertextuality: connecting texts
items.markingKey: Readers, writers and texts; Time and space; Intertextuality: connecting texts. The course is organised into these three areas of exploration.

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "Only books can be studied as texts in English Language and Literature." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Any crafted artefact that communicates meaning – adverts, photographs, websites, speeches, memes – is a text in the course.
items.markingKey: Any crafted artefact that communicates meaning – adverts, photographs, websites, speeches, memes – is a text in the course. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following sponsored advertisement for a skincare serum, shown in a social media feed.

Glow like you mean it.
Clinically shown*: 87% saw brighter skin in 14 days.
Powered by Vitamin C-12, our exclusive molecule from Swiss labs.
Because you deserve skin that tells the truth about you.
#NoFilterNeeded – Tap to shop. Free delivery today only.
*Survey of 64 women, self-reported results.

Explain which features of the extract mark it as a particular text type.
items.answer: It is a advertisement. Conventions: a headline or slogan, an image, a brand name or logo, persuasive copy and a call to action. In this text, for example: "87% saw brighter skin in 14 days" (statistic) and the asterisk linking the claim to the footnote, each used to serve the text's purpose for its audience.
items.markingKey: It is a advertisement. Conventions: a headline or slogan, an image, a brand name or logo, persuasive copy and a call to action. In this text, for example: "87% saw brighter skin in 14 days" (statistic) and the asterisk linking the claim to the footnote, each used to serve the text's purpose for its audience. Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel translated from Arabic (an original passage written for study).

In my father's house, the men ate first. My mother called this respect. My aunt, who had studied law in Cairo before her marriage, called it nothing at all; she simply ate standing in the kitchen doorway, her plate in one hand and a newspaper in the other, so that she belonged to neither room.

Outline the conventions of the text type used here, with examples from the extract.
items.answer: It is a extract in translation. Conventions: a source text rendered in another language, with the translator's choices sometimes visible in notes. In this text, for example: "ate standing in the kitchen doorway" (symbol), each used to serve the text's purpose for its audience.
items.markingKey: It is a extract in translation. Conventions: a source text rendered in another language, with the translator's choices sometimes visible in notes. In this text, for example: "ate standing in the kitchen doorway" (symbol), each used to serve the text's purpose for its audience. Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Choose one literary work and one non-literary text type you have studied. Explain how each makes meaning, and evaluate whether the same analytical vocabulary works for both.
items.answer: Indicative content: identify conventions of each; show shared tools (diction, imagery, structure, point of view) and different ones (layout, image, typography for the non-literary); judge that the vocabulary overlaps but non-literary analysis needs visual and contextual terms.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: identify conventions of each; show shared tools (diction, imagery, structure, point of view) and different ones (layout, image, typography for the non-literary); judge that the vocabulary overlaps but non-literary analysis needs visual and contextual terms.

items.stem: Briefly explain why studying a "body of work" is useful for non-literary texts.
items.answer: Single non-literary texts can be short; a body of work (by one creator or one text type) allows students to identify patterns, recurring techniques and changes over time.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Single non-literary texts can be short; a body of work (by one creator or one text type) allows students to identify patterns, recurring techniques and changes over time. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a non-literary text and a literary work.
items.answer: A literary work is an imaginative or crafted work of literature studied whole (novel, play, poetry collection), usually valued for its aesthetic qualities; a non-literary text is an everyday or functional text (advert, speech, article) whose primary aim is often to inform, persuade or entertain in a specific context.
items.markingKey: A literary work is an imaginative or crafted work of literature studied whole (novel, play, poetry collection), usually valued for its aesthetic qualities; a non-literary text is an everyday or functional text (advert, speech, article) whose primary aim is often to inform, persuade or entertain in a specific context. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Distinguishing literary from non-literary texts is becoming impossible in the digital age." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The boundary is porous but still useful: it describes tendencies of purpose and form, not rigid categories.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: memes, Instagram poetry and fan fiction blur boundaries; graphic novels and literary non-fiction combine features. Arguments against: conventions and purposes still differ (a campaign aims to change behaviour; a novel invites interpretation); the course itself relies on the distinction for assessment. Supported judgement: The boundary is porous but still useful: it describes tendencies of purpose and form, not rigid categories. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem: How many course concepts are there in Language A: Language and Literature?
items.answer: Seven
items.markingKey: Seven. The seven concepts are identity, culture, creativity, communication, perspective, transformation and representation.

items.stem: Priya writes: "Creativity only refers to how original the writer is." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Creativity also includes the reader's active, imaginative role in constructing meaning and the creative reuse of conventions.
items.markingKey: Creativity also includes the reader's active, imaginative role in constructing meaning and the creative reuse of conventions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain how the concept of "perspective" applies to both writers and readers.
items.answer: Writers present events from a chosen point of view, and readers interpret texts through their own experiences and values, so meaning arises from the meeting of two perspectives. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Writers present events from a chosen point of view, and readers interpret texts through their own experiences and values, so meaning arises from the meeting of two perspectives. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a city mayor at the opening of a public library in a multilingual neighbourhood.

Friends, neighbours – bienvenidos, karibu, welcome. Some people say libraries are relics, that everything we need is on our phones. But a phone cannot hold a child's hand through her first chapter book. A phone does not stay open late for the night-shift nurse who wants to finish her degree. This building belongs to you: to every language spoken on these streets, and to every language not yet learned.

Which of the seven course concepts is most relevant to this text? Justify your choice with reference to the text.
items.answer: Community and culture: the library is represented as a shared cultural space that holds many languages.
items.markingKey: Community and culture: the library is represented as a shared cultural space that holds many languages. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following letter to the editor of a regional newspaper in northern England.

Sir, – Your columnist last week described our local accent as 'charming but unprofessional'. I have been a nurse for twenty-two years. I have said 'you're alright, love' to frightened patients at three in the morning, and not one has asked for my vowels to be adjusted. Accent is not a skill deficit. It is where we come from, and where many of your readers still live.

How could this text be used to explore the concept of identity in your learner portfolio?
items.answer: Identity: accent is presented as part of personal and regional identity.
items.markingKey: Identity: accent is presented as part of personal and regional identity. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: Choose two of the seven course concepts. Explain how each could help you analyse a speech you have studied, and evaluate which is more illuminating.
items.answer: Indicative content: define each concept; apply to specific features of the speech (e.g. perspective – whose experience is voiced; communication – rhetorical devices for a live audience); reasoned judgement about which reveals more.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: define each concept; apply to specific features of the speech (e.g. perspective – whose experience is voiced; communication – rhetorical devices for a live audience); reasoned judgement about which reveals more.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "perspective"?
options: A category of non-literary text with recognisable conventions, such as an advertisement, speech, opinion column, infographic or blog
An individual collection of a student's responses to the texts and works studied, kept throughout the course; it is not assessed but supports all assessments
Anything that can be read or interpreted for meaning – written, spoken, visual or multimodal – produced by someone for an audience and purpose
The particular point of view from which a text presents its subject, and the viewpoints readers bring to it
items.answer: The particular point of view from which a text presents its subject, and the viewpoints readers bring to it
items.markingKey: D. "perspective" is the particular point of view from which a text presents its subject, and the viewpoints readers bring to it.

items.stem: Explain the difference between representation and perspective.
items.answer: Representation concerns how a text constructs its subject (e.g. how women are shown); perspective concerns the point of view from which it is presented or read. A single perspective produces a particular representation.
items.markingKey: Representation concerns how a text constructs its subject (e.g. how women are shown); perspective concerns the point of view from which it is presented or read. A single perspective produces a particular representation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Creativity only refers to how original the writer is." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Creativity also includes the reader's active, imaginative role in constructing meaning and the creative reuse of conventions.
items.markingKey: Creativity also includes the reader's active, imaginative role in constructing meaning and the creative reuse of conventions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following infographic from a national youth health service website, described in words.

[Headline: 'WHERE DOES YOUR PHONE SLEEP?'] [Two bars side by side: a short purple bar labelled 'Phone in bedroom: 7 h 1 min average sleep' and a taller bar labelled 'Phone outside bedroom: 8 h 3 min'.]
[Small moon icons fill the taller bar.] 'Each extra hour of evening screen time = about 15 minutes later to sleep.'
[Footer:] 'Charge it outside. Sleep inside.' Source: national youth sleep survey, 2025 (illustrative figures).

Discuss how the text could be used to explore TWO of the seven course concepts, beginning with communication.
items.answer: Communication: complex data is communicated quickly through visual comparison.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "exploratory entry"?
options: A single work of literature (a novel, a play, a collection of poems or short stories, a work of literary non-fiction) studied in full in the course
The process by which meaning passes between a text's producer and its audience, affected by medium, context and convention
An individual collection of a student's responses to the texts and works studied, kept throughout the course; it is not assessed but supports all assessments
A learner portfolio entry that tests ideas, asks questions or experiments with creative responses to a text
items.answer: A learner portfolio entry that tests ideas, asks questions or experiments with creative responses to a text
items.markingKey: D. "exploratory entry" is a learner portfolio entry that tests ideas, asks questions or experiments with creative responses to a text.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a reflective entry and an analytical entry.
items.answer: An analytical entry examines how textual features create meaning (e.g. annotating imagery); a reflective entry considers the student's own response and learning (e.g. how their view of a character changed).
items.markingKey: An analytical entry examines how textual features create meaning (e.g. annotating imagery); a reflective entry considers the student's own response and learning (e.g. how their view of a character changed). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Learner portfolio entries should only be written." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Entries can be multimodal – mind maps, annotated images, audio recordings or videos.
items.markingKey: Entries can be multimodal – mind maps, annotated images, audio recordings or videos. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Design an exploratory learner portfolio entry that connects a poem you have studied with an advertisement on the same global issue. List three things you would include.
items.answer: Possible items: an annotated copy of both texts; a table comparing how each represents the issue; a question for further inquiry (e.g. "Why does the advert simplify what the poem complicates?").
items.markingKey: Possible items: an annotated copy of both texts; a table comparing how each represents the issue; a question for further inquiry (e.g. "Why does the advert simplify what the poem complicates?").

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a campaigner for women's suffrage at a public meeting in Manchester, 1912 (an original pastiche written for study).

Gentlemen of the press, you call us unreasonable. Very well. Was it reasonable that my mother paid taxes on a shop she ran for thirty years, yet could not vote for the men who spent them? Was it reasonable that the law counted her as a citizen when it came to paying, and as a child when it came to choosing? We have asked politely for forty years. Politeness has been answered with silence. We shall not be silent any longer.

Write the opening of a learner portfolio entry on this text, identifying the global issue it raises and one question you would like to investigate.
items.answer: Political power and gender equality: who is allowed a voice in democracy. Supporting feature: "Was it reasonable that my mother paid taxes" (rhetorical question) – the question turns the press's accusation back on the law and expects the answer "no".
items.markingKey: Political power and gender equality: who is allowed a voice in democracy. Supporting feature: "Was it reasonable that my mother paid taxes" (rhetorical question) – the question turns the press's accusation back on the law and expects the answer "no". Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.answer: An individual collection of a student's responses to the texts and works studied, kept throughout the course; it is not assessed but supports all assessments

items.stem: Explain why keeping a learner portfolio helps with the Individual Oral.
items.answer: The portfolio records global issues and connections between literary and non-literary texts as they are studied, so students can find suitable extracts and a focus for the oral.

items.stem: Write a reflective learner portfolio entry (about 150 words) in which you consider how your first impression of a character in a novel you are studying changed after the second chapter.
items.answer: Indicative content: states the first impression and the evidence for it; identifies the moment and the authorial choice that changed it; reflects on what the change reveals about the writer's method and the student's assumptions.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: states the first impression and the evidence for it; identifies the moment and the authorial choice that changed it; reflects on what the change reveals about the writer's method and the student's assumptions.

items.answer: Entries can be multimodal – mind maps, annotated images, audio recordings or videos.

items.stem: Write a learner portfolio entry of about 300 words that compares how a literary work and a non-literary text you have studied represent the same global issue, ending with a question for further exploration.
items.answer: Indicative content: clearly identified global issue; at least two specific features from each text; comparison of methods and effects; an open, inquiring question. Markband: insight, specific reference, organisation, clear register.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: clearly identified global issue; at least two specific features from each text; comparison of methods and effects; an open, inquiring question. Markband: insight, specific reference, organisation, clear register.

items.answer: An adaptation transforms a source text into a new medium or context, and studying what is changed reveals both texts' assumptions and the new audience's values.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a genre and a text type.
items.answer: A text type is a category of text defined by its function and conventions (e.g. a speech, an infographic); a genre is a category within literature or media defined by subject and style (e.g. tragedy, science fiction). One text type can contain many genres.

items.stem:
Read the following poem 'For My Grandfather, Who Fixed Radios' (an original poem written for study).

For My Grandfather, Who Fixed Radios

His hands knew static the way a farmer knows rain:
patient, listening for the voice inside the noise.
The day he died, I turned the dial
through every station in the city,
and every one was speaking,
and none of them was him.

Write the opening of a learner portfolio entry on this text, identifying the global issue it raises and one question you would like to investigate.
items.answer: Grief, memory and family. Supporting feature: "the voice inside the noise" (metaphor) – it captures repair work and the speaker's search for meaning in grief.
items.markingKey: Grief, memory and family. Supporting feature: "the voice inside the noise" (metaphor) – it captures repair work and the speaker's search for meaning in grief. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following three-panel comic strip, described in words.

[Panel 1: a world leader at a podium declares, 'We pledge to reach net zero by 2050!' Applause lines fill the background.]
[Panel 2: a polar bear on a shrinking ice floe raises a paw: 'Question – what's the plan for this summer?']
[Panel 3: the leader, sweating, looks away: 'Next question.']

Explain which features of the extract mark it as a particular text type.
items.answer: It is a cartoon. Conventions: a single image or panels, caricature, captions or speech bubbles and visual exaggeration for comment. In this text, for example: "a polar bear on a shrinking ice floe raises a paw" (anthropomorphism) and the three-panel set-up, question and punchline, each used to serve the text's purpose for its audience.

items.stem:
Read the following food blog post by a second-generation Ghanaian-British writer.

My mum never measured anything. 'Small pepper,' she'd say, and my eyes would water for an hour. Writing her jollof recipe down for you feels like a betrayal – like pinning a butterfly. But she is getting older, and I am scared of forgetting. So here it is, in grams and millilitres, with all the love that won't fit in brackets.

How could this text be used to explore the concept of transformation in your learner portfolio?
items.answer: Transformation: oral family knowledge is transformed into a written, measured recipe.
items.markingKey: Transformation: oral family knowledge is transformed into a written, measured recipe. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel translated from Japanese, with a translator's note (an original passage written for study).

At the door, Grandmother said, 'Itte rasshai,' as she did every morning, and I answered, 'Ittekimasu,' though we both knew I was not coming back for a long time.
[Translator's note: these are the fixed phrases said when someone leaves home – roughly 'go and come back' and 'I will go and come back'. I have kept the Japanese because no English farewell carries the same promise of return.]

Write the opening of a learner portfolio entry on this text, identifying the global issue it raises and one question you would like to investigate.
items.answer: Language, culture and what is lost in translation. Supporting feature: "'Itte rasshai' ... 'Ittekimasu'" (untranslated words) – keeping the Japanese preserves cultural specificity.
items.markingKey: Language, culture and what is lost in translation. Supporting feature: "'Itte rasshai' ... 'Ittekimasu'" (untranslated words) – keeping the Japanese preserves cultural specificity. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The concept of representation is more useful for non-literary texts than for literary works."
items.answer: It is equally useful; it simply operates more overtly in non-literary texts and more subtly in literary ones.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a literary work and a non-literary text.
items.answer: A literary work is an imaginative or crafted work of literature studied whole (novel, play, poetry collection), usually valued for its aesthetic qualities; a non-literary text is an everyday or functional text (advert, speech, article) whose primary aim is often to inform, persuade or entertain in a specific context.
items.markingKey: A literary work is an imaginative or crafted work of literature studied whole (novel, play, poetry collection), usually valued for its aesthetic qualities; a non-literary text is an everyday or functional text (advert, speech, article) whose primary aim is often to inform, persuade or entertain in a specific context. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between identity and culture.
items.answer: Identity is the sense of self of an individual or group; culture is the shared system of practices and values within which identities form. A text may show an individual identity in tension with its culture.
items.markingKey: Identity is the sense of self of an individual or group; culture is the shared system of practices and values within which identities form. A text may show an individual identity in tension with its culture. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kwame writes: "The learner portfolio is a polished essay submitted at the end of the course." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It is an ongoing, varied collection of entries – notes, annotations, creative pieces and reflections – not a single polished essay, and it is not submitted for marking.
items.markingKey: It is an ongoing, varied collection of entries – notes, annotations, creative pieces and reflections – not a single polished essay, and it is not submitted for marking. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why "representation" is a central concept when studying advertisements.
items.answer: Advertisements do not show reality neutrally; they construct versions of people, places and lifestyles to persuade, so analysing representation reveals the values and assumptions they promote.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Advertisements do not show reality neutrally; they construct versions of people, places and lifestyles to persuade, so analysing representation reveals the values and assumptions they promote. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a play (an original extract written for study).

[A kitchen, late evening. A single bulb. AMIRA, 17, sits with a university acceptance letter. Her father, KARIM, enters, still in his work jacket.]
KARIM: You're up late.
AMIRA: (folding the letter quickly) Reading.
KARIM: Reading what?
AMIRA: Nothing. Just – school.
KARIM: (picks up her empty mug, rinses it, his back to her) Your mother would have read everything you wrote. Every word.
[Pause. AMIRA slides the letter under the fruit bowl.]

Write the opening of a learner portfolio entry on this text, identifying the global issue it raises and one question you would like to investigate.
items.answer: Family duty, grief and individual ambition. Supporting feature: "You're up late. / Reading. / Reading what?" (stichomythia) – rapid short exchanges show tension and evasion.
items.markingKey: Family duty, grief and individual ambition. Supporting feature: "You're up late. / Reading. / Reading what?" (stichomythia) – rapid short exchanges show tension and evasion. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: A student claims: "Only books can be studied as texts in English Language and Literature." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Any crafted artefact that communicates meaning – adverts, photographs, websites, speeches, memes – is a text in the course.
items.markingKey: Any crafted artefact that communicates meaning – adverts, photographs, websites, speeches, memes – is a text in the course. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "The seven concepts are themes, so each text has only one concept." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Concepts are lenses, not themes; any text can be explored through several concepts, and the strongest analysis often connects two or more.
items.markingKey: Concepts are lenses, not themes; any text can be explored through several concepts, and the strongest analysis often connects two or more. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following description of Dorothea Lange's photograph 'Migrant Mother' (1936) with its original caption.

[A black-and-white photograph. A woman in worn clothes sits under a tent, her hand raised to her chin, her eyes looking past the camera with a worried expression. Two children lean on her shoulders, faces turned away; a baby lies in her lap. The frame is tight, cutting out the surroundings.]
Caption (US Farm Security Administration file): 'Destitute pea pickers in California. Mother of seven children. Age thirty-two. Nipomo, California.'

In a short learner portfolio note, record the global issue this text engages with and one feature you would analyse.
items.answer: Poverty, representation and the ethics of documentary photography. Supporting feature: "her eyes looking past the camera" (averted gaze) – the gaze into the distance suggests worry about the future rather than a posed portrait.
items.markingKey: Poverty, representation and the ethics of documentary photography. Supporting feature: "her eyes looking past the camera" (averted gaze) – the gaze into the distance suggests worry about the future rather than a posed portrait. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: Amara writes: "Non-literary texts are simpler than literary works and need less analysis." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Non-literary texts can be highly crafted; a short advert may use visual composition, connotation and structure as deliberately as a poem.
items.markingKey: Non-literary texts can be highly crafted; a short advert may use visual composition, connotation and structure as deliberately as a poem. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a campaigner for women's suffrage at a public meeting in Manchester, 1912 (an original pastiche written for study).

Gentlemen of the press, you call us unreasonable. Very well. Was it reasonable that my mother paid taxes on a shop she ran for thirty years, yet could not vote for the men who spent them? Was it reasonable that the law counted her as a citizen when it came to paying, and as a child when it came to choosing? We have asked politely for forty years. Politeness has been answered with silence. We shall not be silent any longer.

Discuss how the text could be used to explore TWO of the seven course concepts, beginning with representation.
items.answer: Representation: the speaker challenges the press's representation of campaigners as unreasonable.
items.markingKey: Representation: the speaker challenges the press's representation of campaigners as unreasonable. Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The learner portfolio is the most important part of the course even though it is not assessed."
items.answer: Its value depends on use: a rich, regular portfolio is central to success, but its importance lies in what it enables rather than in itself.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it underpins every assessment; it develops independent thinking. Arguments against: without marks students may neglect it; assessments test skills that can be developed elsewhere. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Distinguishing literary from non-literary texts is becoming impossible in the digital age."
items.answer: The boundary is porous but still useful: it describes tendencies of purpose and form, not rigid categories.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: memes, Instagram poetry and fan fiction blur boundaries; graphic novels and literary non-fiction combine features. Arguments against: conventions and purposes still differ (a campaign aims to change behaviour; a novel invites interpretation); the course itself relies on the distinction for assessment.
